S069.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
S069.description: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.

subtypes.Intrusive Memories: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.
subtypes.Distressing Dreams: Recurrent distressing dreams in which the content and/or affect of the dream are related to the traumatic event.
subtypes.Dissociative Reactions (Flashbacks): Dissociative reactions (e.g., flashbacks) in which the individual feels or acts as if the traumatic event were recurring.
subtypes.Psychological Distress at Cues: Intense or prolonged psychological distress at exposure to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event.
subtypes.Physiological Reactions to Cues: Marked physiological reactions to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event.

S070.name: Trauma_Avoidance
S070.description: Persistent avoidance of stimuli associated with the traumatic event.

subtypes.Internal Avoidance: Efforts to avoid distressing memories, thoughts, or feelings about or closely associated with the traumatic event.
subtypes.External Avoidance: Efforts to avoid external reminders (people, places, conversations, activities, objects, situations) that arouse distressing memories, thoughts, or feelings.

S076.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
S076.description: Persistent inability to experience positive emotions (e.g., inability to experience happiness, satisfaction, or loving feelings).

subtypes.Anhedonia for Happiness: Unable to feel happiness or joy even when good things happen.
subtypes.Lack of Satisfaction: Unable to experience satisfaction or pride even after achieving something good.
subtypes.Inability to Feel Love: Feeling numb to love or affection towards family or lovers.
subtypes.Emotional Numbness: A state where the mind feels empty and nothing is felt, as if all positive emotions are blocked.

S077.name: Irritability_Aggression
S077.description: Irritable behavior and angry outbursts (with little or no provocation) typically expressed as verbal or physical aggression.

subtypes.Impulsive Anger: Sudden explosions of anger for trivial reasons or no clear reason.
subtypes.Verbal Aggression: Attacking others with shouting, cursing, or blame without holding back.
subtypes.Physical Aggression: Physically attacking people or throwing/breaking objects.
subtypes.Chronic Irritability: A state where nerves are always sharp and sensitive, ready to explode at the slightest touch.

S080.name: Exaggerated_Startle_Response
S080.description: Exaggerated startle response to minor stimuli.

subtypes.Auditory Startle: Startling excessively and flinching physically at sudden noises.
subtypes.Tactile Startle: Being extremely startled by unexpected physical contact.
subtypes.Visual Startle: Being greatly startled and wary of sudden appearances of people or rapid movements.
subtypes.Slow Recovery: Heart pounding and trembling for a long time after being startled, not calming down easily.

S082.name: Depersonalization_Derealization
S082.description: Altered sense of the reality of one's self or surroundings after a traumatic event.

subtypes.Depersonalization: Feeling detached from one's own body or mental processes, as if being an outside observer.
subtypes.Derealization: The surrounding environment feels unreal, dreamlike, distant, or distorted.
subtypes.Time Distortion: Time feels like it has stopped during the traumatic moment, or is perceived as moving extremely slowly or quickly.

symptom.disease_info: Acute Stress Disorder (ASD) is a trauma- and stressor-related condition that emerges within days of exposure to a traumatic event involving actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violation. It is characterized by a cluster of intrusive memories, dissociation, negative mood, avoidance, and arousal symptoms lasting from 3 days to 1 month after the trauma, with associated functional impairment. Clinically, ASD often presents with marked distress, sleep and concentration problems, and difficulty resuming normal roles, and it confers elevated risk for later Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) if symptoms persist or intensify. It is distinguished from normal acute stress reactions by symptom severity, breadth of symptom clusters, and significant interference with social or occupational functioning, and from PTSD primarily by its shorter duration and more immediate temporal relationship to the trauma.

patient.stressor: Guillermo was flying back from a high-stakes negotiation on a red-eye flight when the plane hit sudden, extreme turbulence and dropped sharply, causing oxygen masks to deploy and unsecured items to fly through the cabin. For several minutes, passengers screamed and a flight attendant was thrown against the ceiling before the pilots stabilized the aircraft and announced an emergency landing; Guillermo sat strapped in, convinced they were going to crash, mentally rehearsing what would happen to his family and company. In the six days that followed, his usually precise, ordered routine collapsed—he left strategy meetings abruptly, could not bring himself to enter the company’s high-floor conference room with large windows overlooking the Bay, and began avoiding any discussion of upcoming business travel, which was central to his role. After his chief operating officer found him sitting in his office with the door locked, unable to return to a board meeting after hearing a low rumble from a passing truck that reminded him of the plane’s engines, she insisted he see a psychiatrist that same day through the company’s executive health program.
patient.chief_complaint: “Ever since that near-crash on the plane, every small noise or movement makes me jump out of my skin, and I can’t function in meetings because I’m constantly on edge waiting for something bad to happen.”

S069.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
S069.description: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event.
S069.manifestation: All week these scenes just slam into my head out of nowhere—the masks dropping, the flight attendant hitting the ceiling, people screaming—and for a few seconds I’m right back in that seat, sweating and gripping the armrests like we’re about to die again, even if I’m just sitting at my desk or trying to read email at home.

S070.name: Trauma_Avoidance
S070.description: Persistent avoidance of stimuli associated with the traumatic event.
S070.manifestation: I do everything I can not to think or talk about that flight—if someone mentions planes or travel I cut them off, I make excuses to skip meetings in the top-floor conference room because it feels too much like being up in the air, and I won’t even look at my airline app because I feel sick the second I see a picture of a plane.

S076.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
S076.description: Persistent inability to experience positive emotions (e.g., inability to experience happiness, satisfaction, or loving feelings).
S076.manifestation: Since this happened I feel like somebody flipped a switch inside me—my wife tells me good news about the kids or the company hits a target, and I just sit there numb, like I’m watching someone else’s life and can’t feel any joy or warmth about it at all.

S077.name: Irritability_Aggression
S077.description: Irritable behavior and angry outbursts (with little or no provocation) typically expressed as verbal or physical aggression.
S077.manifestation: I’m on such a short fuse that the smallest thing sets me off—when my assistant asked a routine question about rescheduling a trip, I snapped and barked at her to just handle it and leave me alone, and later that day I slammed my hand on the table in a meeting because someone’s pen kept clicking and I thought I was going to explode.

S080.name: Exaggerated_Startle_Response
S080.description: Exaggerated startle response to minor stimuli.
S080.manifestation: Now every little sound or movement makes me jump out of my skin—if a truck rumbles past the building or someone rolls their chair behind me, I physically jerk, my heart starts pounding like it did on the plane, and it takes me several minutes to calm down enough to follow what anyone is saying in the room.

S082.name: Depersonalization_Derealization
S082.description: Altered sense of the reality of one's self or surroundings after a traumatic event.
S082.manifestation: There are moments, especially in the office or lying in bed at night, when I feel like I’m watching myself from across the room and the world looks kind of flat and unreal, like I’m stuck in a bad movie of that flight and not fully back in my own body yet.

add_requirements.functional_impairment: In the past week I’ve walked out of key meetings, dodged travel-related decisions that are central to my job, and gone home early because I just can’t think straight or stay in the room, to the point where my COO has started quietly taking over parts of my role.
add_requirements.duration: All of this started right after that near-crash on the plane about six days ago and has been going on continuously since then.
